title: Fulfill your contracts
hookLine: O you who believe, fulfill your obligations (5:1)

cards: The fifth surah is al-Ma'idah, the Table Spread, named for a story near its end, where the disciples of Isa ask for a table of food to come down from heaven. Tradition places it among the last surahs revealed.

And it opens with a command of two Arabic words, three in Pickthall's English, right after the address. No story, no setting. Just a sentence that covers a marriage, a mortgage, a handshake and a treaty.

teach.b: Here it is, 5:1, in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." The Arabic for undertakings is al-'uqud, contracts, plural of 'aqd. Arabic dictionaries trace it to a root for tying a knot.
A contract is a knot tied between two parties, and the verse says: don't let it slip.

Commentators read 'uqud widely: the covenant between a person and God, and every agreement between people, marriage, sale, rent, employment, oaths, treaties. Marriage itself is called 'aqd al-nikah, the knot of marriage.
In 17:34, the Qur'an adds that the covenant will be asked about. The Prophet ﷺ faced a hard test of it at Hudaybiyyah.
He had just agreed a treaty with the Quraysh of Mecca, and one term was painful: anyone who came over from Mecca to the Muslims without permission would be sent back.

The ink was barely dry when a young Muslim named Abu Jandal stumbled into the camp in chains, escaped from Mecca, begging not to be returned. His own father, Suhayl, was the Meccan who had negotiated the treaty.
The companions were in anguish. The Prophet kept the terms, and told Abu Jandal to be patient, that God would make a way out for him.

teach.h: A KNOT THAT HOLDS WHEN IT PINCHES
teach.b: The sira reports that the way did open: before long, the Quraysh themselves asked for that clause to be dropped.
A contract kept only when it's convenient isn't really a knot. The verse asks for one that holds even when it pinches.

how: Muslims treat contracts as religious obligations: marriage is concluded by an 'aqd, Islamic commercial law rests on honoring agreements, and 5:1 is often quoted on keeping promises and treaties.

a contract: a knot tied between two

games.q: you've just signed a treaty. a young believer arrives in chains, begging not to be sent back, and the terms say he must be. what did the Prophet do?
o: keep the terms, and tell him God would make a way out.
games.why: he kept the agreement. the sira reports that before long the Quraysh themselves asked to drop that clause.

practice: List in your mind the knots you've tied: a lease, a job, a promise to a friend, a deadline, a commitment to someone you love, even I'll call you back.
Notice, without punishing yourself, which are holding and which have quietly slipped, and which one has become inconvenient.

wordCard.voice: 'Aqd, a knot, a contract tied between two parties. Awfu bil-'uqud: keep the knots you've tied, with God and with people, the opening of al-Ma'idah, 5:1. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: fulfill the contracts (5:1); 'uqud, plural of 'aqd, a knot.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the contract. Small knots count too, like I'll call you back. That's day three hundred eighty-eight.
